newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss money traders see rates staying steady.
newsitem.headline: Swiss money traders see rates staying steady.

text.p: Swiss money rates will probably remain steady despite latest data showing a further decline in the unemployment rate to 5.5 percent in April, money traders said.
The jobless rate was 5.7 percent in January and February, and 5.6 percent in March.
Some money market traders wonder if short-term rates have begun to bottom out, given signs of minor economic improvement. But so far none seems to expect rates to rise.
"Maybe we have seen the lowest levels" (in terms of rates), said one trader at a major Swiss bank.
At a second big bank, however, a trader said it was too soon to talk of changes in rates.
"Clearly one can say the room is a bit limited to the downside because we are so low (in terms of rates), but there is still room," he said.
"The Swiss National Bank (SNB) has done normal operations. It is still present in the market. I don't see any major changes," he added.
Traders said the SNB added liquidity Friday to May 22 at 1-5/8 percent, the rate set in recent operations. Tomorrow/next money was quoted at 1-1/2 to 1-5/8 percent this morning, also little changed.
The economic outlook remains uncertain, and analysts say data showing its progress are likely to be mixed.
Bank forecasts indicate Swiss first quarter gross domestic product (GDP), expected to be released between June 10 and 15, may be slightly up from the final quarter of 1996.
But it could show a slight decline from first quarter 1996 which had an extra day because it was a leap year.
Economists said Swiss consumer demand remains weak, and a rise in the Swiss franc could hurt recovery.
At a third bank, a trader said Swiss short-term rates could bottom out, but this did not mean rates would go higher. He said the market remained well-supplied with liquidity.
The SNB has said it is keeping an eye on inflation, but has stressed that it has no plans to tighten, a move which would have the undesirable effect of boosting the franc.
Bruno Gehrig, one of the SNB's three board members, told a business forum last week that the SNB would create problems by easing excessively.
Asked whether there was a need to tighten, Gehrig reiterated earlier SNB statements that currently there was no need for monetary tightening.
He said Swiss economic activity was nowhere near the level of growth which could be sustained on a long-term basis. He said that level was likely to be somewhere around two percent.

SNB chairman Hans Meyer is scheduled to give a speech on May 14. He will probably focus on Swiss plans to form a humanitarian fund. Any comments he makes about monetary policy are likely to be as even-handed as previous SNB comments.

"The (money) market is well-supplied. They (the SNB) definitely don't want to signal they are reversing. But we will hear officials say again and again in the future that they will act pro-actively," one trader said.
-- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
